analogy.p: Imagine two houses of cards on a table, one built carefully with extra supports and the other quickly with no supports. If you shake the table, the strong one may stay up while the weak one collapses. The shaking is the **hazard**, the houses are the **buildings and communities**, and the difference in construction is the difference in **development and preparation**. A big shake (high magnitude) is more likely to wreck both, but a small shake right under the table (shallow, close focus) can still knock down a weak house. The analogy breaks down because real disasters also involve people's responses afterwards (rescue, aid, rebuilding), which cards cannot show.
analogy.t: A house of cards on a shaking table

bullets: A **primary effect** is the immediate result of the event itself (for example buildings collapsing in the shaking). A **secondary effect** happens later, as a result of the primary effects (for example fires, disease or lost jobs).

An **immediate response** is what people do in the hours, days and first weeks (for example search and rescue). A **long-term response** is what happens in the months and years after (for example rebuilding and new building rules).
Effects are usually sorted into **social** (people), **economic** (money and jobs) and **environmental** (landscape and habitats) effects.
The main idea for the exam: the same hazard has **different impacts** because of **level of development**, **preparedness**, **building quality**, **population density**, **depth and magnitude**.
The two case studies make a **contrast**: a larger magnitude in a poor country caused far more deaths and lasting damage than a smaller one in a rich country, but magnitude is not the only reason.
Examiners reward **specific facts**: the name, date, magnitude, number of deaths and cost, and place names. General statements like 'many people died' only get low marks.
core.h: What the spec asks and the big ideas
core.p: AQA wants you to understand the **effects** of tectonic hazards and the **responses** to them, and to use **two case studies**: one of a tectonic hazard in a low income country (LIC) or newly emerging economy (NEE) and one in a high income country (HIC). The case studies must show the primary and secondary effects, the immediate and long-term responses, and how and why the impact differs between richer and poorer places. This page uses the 2015 Nepal earthquake (LIC) and the 2011 Christchurch earthquake (HIC), which are the standard pair. If your teacher used a different pair (for example Chile 2010 or Japan 2011) revise those instead and use this page for the method.

bullets: **Magnitude** is measured with a seismograph on the **Richter scale**, which is logarithmic: each whole number is about 10 times more shaking, so a magnitude 8 quake shakes the ground 100 times more than a magnitude 6.
A **shallow focus** (less than about 70 km) means the waves travel a shorter distance to the surface and cause greater damage than a deep earthquake of the same magnitude.
**Ground type** matters: loose, wet sand or silt can behave like a liquid when shaken (**liquefaction**), which makes buildings tilt, sink or collapse. Solid rock transmits shaking less.
**Time of day** matters: an earthquake in the middle of the day can kill many people in offices and schools; one at night can trap more people in their homes.
**Aftershocks** are smaller earthquakes that follow the main shock for days, weeks or months. They make damaged buildings collapse and slow rescue work.
A **tsunami** can follow an earthquake under or near the sea (see below).

Exam tip: when asked 'why did the earthquake cause so much damage?' pick several factors from the list and link each to a result, for example 'The focus was shallow, so strong shaking reached the surface, causing buildings to collapse'.
core.h: How earthquakes happen, and what makes some more damaging
core.p: An earthquake happens when stress that builds up where two plates are stuck together is suddenly released as **seismic waves**. The place underground where it starts is the **focus** and the point directly above on the surface is the **epicentre**. The shaking is strongest at the epicentre and gets weaker with distance. The damage depends on several factors, not just how large the earthquake is. These include the **magnitude** (measured on the Richter or moment magnitude scale), the **depth of focus** (shallow means more shaking), the **distance** from the epicentre to people, the **type of ground**, and the **quality of buildings**.

bullets: **Lava flows**: streams of molten rock. They move slowly so people can usually escape, but they destroy buildings, roads and farmland in their path.

**Ash clouds** and **tephra**: ash is made of tiny pieces of rock and glass. It can bury buildings (the weight causes roofs to collapse), damage crops, cause breathing problems and close airports because it can damage jet engines (for example the 2010 Eyjafjallajokull eruption in Iceland).

**Pyroclastic flows**: fast, extremely hot clouds of ash, gas and rock that rush down the slopes, often faster than 100 km/h and hundreds of degrees Celsius. They are the biggest killers and nobody can outrun them.
**Lahars**: fast-moving mudflows of volcanic ash mixed with water from rain or melting snow and ice. They can travel far down river valleys and bury towns.
**Volcanic gases**: carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and others. They can poison people and animals and can cause acid rain.
**Secondary effects**: lahars, landslides, floods, and a loss of farming land for years. However, volcanic ash weathers into **very fertile soil**, which is one reason people live near volcanoes.
Volcanic eruptions rarely kill as many people as earthquakes, but they can disrupt air travel and the climate across the world.
core.p: Volcanic eruptions can have many different hazards, and the type depends on the volcano and its magma. Explosive eruptions from composite volcanoes are the most dangerous because they happen with little warning and send out fast-moving hazards. You should be able to name the hazards and link each to its effects. Some hazards are **primary** (from the eruption itself) and some are **secondary** (caused later).

bullets: **Cause**: a powerful earthquake (usually magnitude 7 or more) under the sea that moves the sea floor vertically. Volcanic eruptions and underwater landslides can also trigger tsunamis.
**Speed and height**: fast and low in deep water, slow and tall in shallow water near the coast.
**Warning sign**: the sea sometimes **draws back** a long way before the first wave arrives. People who go to look can be caught.
**Effects**: coastal communities are flooded, people drown, buildings and boats are swept away, farmland is contaminated with salt water and infrastructure is destroyed.
Example: the 2011 earthquake off Japan (magnitude 9.0) caused a huge tsunami that killed about 18,000 people and damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station.
**Responses**: tsunami warning systems (ocean buoys and sirens), evacuation routes and high ground, sea walls and public education.
core.p: A **tsunami** is a series of very long sea waves triggered by a sudden movement of the sea floor, most commonly a large earthquake at a destructive margin where the sea floor is thrust upwards. The water above is displaced and spreads out in all directions as waves. In the deep ocean the waves are low (less than a metre) and travel extremely fast, often at speeds of several hundred kilometres per hour, so ships may not notice them. When the waves reach shallow water near the coast they slow down, bunch up and grow in height, sometimes to over 10 metres, and can flood far inland.

bullets: **Primary effects** of an earthquake: ground shaking, collapse of buildings and bridges, roads and railways destroyed, people killed or injured, water, gas and electricity supplies cut, ground cracks.

**Secondary effects** of an earthquake: fires (broken gas pipes), landslides and avalanches, tsunamis, liquefaction, disease (from dirty water and poor sanitation), shortages of food and water, homelessness, loss of jobs and trade.
**Social effects**: deaths, injuries, homelessness, damaged schools and hospitals, disease, psychological stress and loss of cultural sites.
**Economic effects**: cost of repairing and rebuilding, businesses closed, jobs lost, loss of tourism, farm damage, insurance claims, and rising national debt.
**Environmental effects**: landslides, damaged habitats, polluted rivers (broken sewers), changed landscape (new cracks, lakes blocked by landslides) and fires.
A common mistake is to put an effect in the wrong group. 'Fire caused by broken gas pipes' is **secondary**, not primary, because it happens as a result of the shaking.
In 6-mark questions you should say who is affected, in what way, and how serious it is.
core.h: Primary and secondary effects, and social, economic and environmental effects
core.p: In a case study you must give both primary and secondary effects, and ideally sort them into social, economic and environmental effects. Primary effects happen at the moment of the earthquake or eruption, while secondary effects follow from them. Being able to classify effects correctly is an easy way to gain marks. Always add a specific example or a number for each point.

bullets: **Immediate**: search and rescue teams and sniffer dogs looking for survivors; first aid and field hospitals; emergency shelter such as tents; clean drinking water, food and blankets; evacuating people from danger.
**Immediate**: restoring communication, clearing roads, and temporary electricity and water supplies. International aid and emergency funding are often requested.
**Long-term**: rebuilding homes, schools, hospitals and roads; **stricter building codes** so new buildings are earthquake-resistant; relocating people from unsafe areas.
**Long-term**: restoring jobs and business (including tourism), improving **monitoring and warning systems**, training and preparation (earthquake drills) and long-term health and mental health care.
**Aid** can be short-term (emergency food and shelter) or long-term (development projects). It may come from governments, NGOs such as the Red Cross, or the United Nations.
In poorer countries the response is slowed by weak infrastructure (blocked roads, poor communication) and by a lack of equipment and money, and depends heavily on **international aid**.
In richer countries the response is usually quicker and better organised, funded by taxes and **insurance**, but rebuilding can still take many years.
core.p: Responses are the actions taken by governments, charities, organisations and local people to deal with a hazard. **Immediate responses** take place in the first hours, days and weeks, with the aim of saving lives and meeting basic needs. **Long-term responses** take place over months and years and aim to repair damage, reduce future risk and help the area recover. How effective the responses are depends on how wealthy the country is, how well prepared it was, and how much help it gets from outside.

bullets: **Building quality**: HICs have strict building codes and many buildings are designed to withstand shaking; in LICs many homes are built from unreinforced brick, stone or mud and collapse easily.
**Wealth and preparedness**: HICs have emergency plans, drills, warning systems and insured buildings; LICs often cannot afford these.
**Emergency services and healthcare**: more ambulances, trained rescue teams and hospitals in HICs, so fewer deaths and quicker rescue.
**Infrastructure and access**: remote mountainous areas in LICs can be cut off by landslides, so aid cannot get there quickly.
**Population density and urbanisation**: crowded cities with poor housing (informal settlements) increase deaths in any country.
**Governance and corruption**: weak government can slow aid and rebuilding.

**Do not generalise**: some HICs still suffer major losses (the economic cost of an earthquake can be larger in a rich country because buildings and property are worth more) while deaths are lower. Use this idea for evaluation marks.
core.h: Why impacts and responses differ between countries
core.p: The same tectonic event can be a disaster in one place and a manageable emergency in another. AQA expects you to **explain** why, using development as the main idea. In richer countries people have more money to put into **prediction, protection and planning** before a hazard, and they have more resources for emergency response after it. In poorer countries, many people live in weaker housing, there are fewer emergency services, and recovery relies heavily on outside help.

bullets: **Primary effects**: around **9,000 people died** and about **22,000 were injured**. Around **500,000 homes were destroyed** and many more were damaged, along with schools, hospitals and historic temples in Kathmandu valley, including the Dharahara tower.

**Secondary effects**: **landslides** and **avalanches** blocked roads to remote villages and killed people (for example an avalanche at Everest base camp killed 19 climbers); aftershocks caused more collapses and about 200 more deaths on 12 May.

**Social effects**: millions of people were affected and many were left homeless, living in tents as the monsoon approached; the risk of disease rose because of damaged sanitation; many children missed school.
**Economic effects**: damage was estimated at roughly US$7 billion, a very large share of the country's annual GDP; tourism, a major source of income, fell; farming was disrupted.

**Immediate responses**: international rescue teams and aid from India, China, the UK and others; field hospitals, tents, food and water; helicopters to reach remote villages; the Nepalese army and local people dug for survivors by hand.

**Problems with the response**: many roads were blocked, Kathmandu airport was overwhelmed by aid flights, supplies were slow to reach mountain villages, and the government was criticised for being slow.

**Long-term responses**: a national reconstruction authority was set up and gave grants to households to rebuild; new building codes with earthquake-resistant designs (for example reinforced materials); training builders; and rebuilding of heritage sites. Rebuilding was slow and many families were still waiting years later.
core.p: Nepal is a **low income country** (LIC) in South Asia, in the Himalayas, with a GDP per person of well under US$1,000 per year at the time. It lies on the **collision margin** between the Indian plate and the Eurasian plate. On 25 April 2015 a magnitude **7.8** earthquake struck, with its epicentre in the Gorkha district about 80 km north-west of the capital Kathmandu. The focus was shallow (less than about 20 km deep) and the shaking was felt across the country and in neighbouring India, China and Bangladesh. A magnitude 7.3 aftershock followed on 12 May.

bullets: **Primary effects**: **185 people died** and about 2,000 were injured. It happened at lunchtime, when the city centre was busy. The CTV building collapsed, killing 115 people. About 100,000 houses were damaged and buildings in the centre, including the cathedral, were badly damaged.

**Secondary effects**: widespread **liquefaction** covered streets and homes with silt and water and damaged roads, water and sewage pipes; rockfalls and landslides in the hills; power and water supplies were cut for many households.

**Social effects**: thousands left the city, many people were homeless or lived in temporary housing, and stress and mental health problems increased. Thousands of homes were in the 'red zone' where land was too damaged to rebuild.

**Economic effects**: the costliest disaster in New Zealand history, around NZ$40 billion (a large share of the country's GDP); much of the city centre was closed for years; businesses were lost, but much of the cost was covered by **insurance**.

**Immediate responses**: urban search and rescue teams (including from Australia, Japan, the UK and the USA) arrived quickly; the centre was cordoned off; emergency shelters were set up; water tankers, portable toilets and food; a state of national emergency was declared.

**Long-term responses**: a recovery authority (CERA) was set up to manage rebuilding; thousands of damaged buildings were demolished; temporary shops were built in shipping containers; new building rules and designs such as base isolation were introduced.
The relatively low death toll shows the benefit of strong building rules and preparedness, though the large economic cost and the slow recovery show that even a rich country struggles.
core.p: New Zealand is a **high income country** (HIC) in the Pacific, with a GDP per person above US$30,000 and strict building codes. It lies across the boundary between the Pacific and Australian plates, so earthquakes are a known risk, and the country is well prepared for them. On 22 February 2011 at 12:51 pm a magnitude **6.3** earthquake struck close to Christchurch, the South Island's biggest city. The epicentre was only about 10 km from the city centre and the focus was very shallow (about 5 km), so the shaking at the surface was extremely strong. It was an aftershock of the much larger magnitude 7.1 Darfield earthquake in September 2010, which had caused no deaths but had already weakened many buildings.

bullets: **Deaths and injuries**: very many more in Nepal (about 9,000 deaths) than in Christchurch (185). Reasons: Nepal had weaker housing, a more remote and mountainous area, fewer emergency services.

**Economic cost**: far greater in absolute terms in Christchurch (about NZ$40 billion) because of expensive buildings and infrastructure, but in Nepal the damage was a larger share of the total economy and was harder to recover from because Nepal has less insurance and wealth.

**Immediate response**: Christchurch had well-practised emergency services and rescue teams in hours; Nepal relied heavily on international aid and its response was slowed by blocked roads and a lack of equipment.
**Long-term response**: Christchurch used insurance and government funding and a dedicated recovery authority; Nepal needed international aid and grants, and rebuilding was slow.
**Magnitude was not the only factor**: shallow depth, close to a city, liquefaction (Christchurch) versus landslides and weak buildings (Nepal).

To get top marks, use comparative words such as 'whereas', 'in contrast', 'however', 'both', and finish with a judgement, for example 'Development explains the difference in deaths more than magnitude'.
core.p: AQA likes questions that ask you to compare or contrast, such as 'Compare the effects of earthquakes in an LIC and an HIC'. The best answers use data from both case studies and explain the difference with reasons, not just describing each one separately. Here is the contrast, which is shown in Figure 3: the magnitude 7.8 Nepal earthquake killed around 9,000 people, whereas the smaller magnitude 6.3 Christchurch earthquake killed 185. But remember that the Christchurch epicentre was much closer to a city and shallow, which is why it was so damaging for its size.

bullets: **Reading a bar chart or graph**: read the axis labels and units first. Use the data in your answer (for example 'about 9,000 compared to 185') and say whether it is more or less than something else.
**Percentage**: part divided by whole times 100. Example: if 9,000 people died and 3 million were affected, that is 9,000 divided by 3,000,000 times 100 = 0.3%.
**Percentage change**: (new minus old) divided by old, times 100.
**Ratio or 'how many times greater'**: divide the larger value by the smaller. 9,000 divided by 185 is about 49, so deaths in Nepal were nearly 50 times higher.
**Logarithmic scales**: on the Richter scale, a rise of 1 means about 10 times more shaking, and a rise of 2 means about 100 times more.
**Describing trends**: use words like 'increases', 'decreases', 'fluctuates', 'peaks' with figures to support them.
**Annotated maps**: for a map of damage, describe the pattern (for example 'damage is greatest close to the epicentre and decreases with distance').
**Suggesting reasons** from data: link to development, depth, ground type or time of day.
core.h: Data and graph skills for tectonic hazard questions
core.p: Geography exams contain several marks for skills, including interpreting maps, graphs and data about earthquakes and volcanoes. You may be asked to read values from a bar chart, calculate a mean, percentage or percentage change, or describe a trend. Always quote data from the figure including units, and check the scale before you read it. These skills are examined across all three papers.

bullets: **Case-study pattern**: Where and when (place, date), What happened (plate margin, magnitude, depth), Effects (primary, secondary; social, economic, environmental), Responses (immediate, long-term), and a Conclusion about how effective the response was and why.
Learn **at least six specific facts per case study**: date, magnitude, death toll, injuries, homes destroyed or cost, one named secondary effect and one named response.
A good '6 mark' structure is: two or three **linked** points for effects (with data), two or three for responses (with named actions), and a final comment on development.

For a 9-mark 'to what extent' question, give a balanced argument, such as 'Level of development is the main reason for the difference in deaths, but magnitude and depth also matter', and finish with a conclusion.

Links: **plate margins** (geo.0.1) explain why the hazard occurs; **living in hazardous areas** (geo.0.3) explains why people stay; **monitoring, prediction, protection and planning** (geo.0.4) show how risk is reduced and why preparation reduces the effects.
Link to **population and development** topics: poorer and richer countries differ in their capacity to cope, which is why the same hazard has different risk.
core.h: Exam technique: planning case-study answers (and links to other topics)
core.p: Most of the marks on this topic come from extended answers, usually 4 or 6 marks and sometimes 9 marks with up to 3 extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar (SPaG). To get the top level you need **specific detail** from your case study, accurate terminology, a clear structure and, for 'assess' or 'evaluate' questions, a **judgement**. Plan your answer using a short list before you write.

exam: Command words: 'describe' (say what happened, with data), 'explain' (give reasons using 'because'), 'compare' (similarities and differences with data from both), 'assess' or 'to what extent' (balanced argument and a judgement).
1-mark questions often ask for a definition or a single fact (for example 'what is meant by a primary effect?'). Be precise and short.
2-mark questions: give two separate points, or one point with development (a fact plus a reason, joined by 'which means' or 'because').
4-mark questions on effects or responses need either four distinct points or two points each developed with an example from your case study.
6-mark case study answers should include place names, numbers and a clear structure: effects first, then responses, then a conclusion about development.
Always separate primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses if the question mentions them. The mark scheme will credit each group.
Use the words 'social', 'economic' and 'environmental' as headings in your head and make sure you have at least one point from each.
When comparing the two case studies, write comparative sentences such as 'Whereas in Nepal ..., in Christchurch ...' rather than describing each separately.
For data questions, quote the figures with units, and use a calculation if asked (for example 9,000 divided by 185 is about 49 times).
Explain why impacts differ by naming a factor and linking it: 'Nepal had weaker buildings, so more collapsed and more people died'.
For 9-mark questions add a judgement ('The main reason was ...') and consider a counter-argument.
Check spelling of key terms (earthquake, epicentre, magnitude, liquefaction, tsunami) as SPaG marks may be available on extended answers.

mistakes.r: Give social, economic and environmental effects, and separate primary from secondary, with specific data.
mistakes.w: Effects of an earthquake are only deaths and damaged buildings.

mistakes.r: It is a secondary effect, because it is caused by the primary effect (broken gas pipes) and not by the shaking itself.
mistakes.w: A fire after an earthquake is a primary effect.

mistakes.r: They have fewer deaths and quicker recovery, but can have a larger economic cost (more valuable property). Compare carefully.
mistakes.w: Richer countries have fewer earthquake problems.

mistakes.r: Magnitude was a factor, but development, building quality, remote terrain and limited emergency services explain the high death toll.
mistakes.w: Nepal's earthquake was bigger so it killed more people.

mistakes.r: The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole number is about 10 times more shaking, so magnitude 8 is about 10,000 times more shaking than 4.
mistakes.w: A magnitude 8 is twice as strong as magnitude 4.

mistakes.r: Effects are what the hazard does; responses are what people do about it. Do not mix them up.
mistakes.w: Responses are the same as effects.

mistakes.r: Include date, place, magnitude, numbers and named actions; marks are for specific detail.
mistakes.w: The case study answer is a general description with no facts.

mistakes.r: Rebuilding is a long-term response. Immediate means rescue, shelter, food, water and medical care.
A tsunami is caused by a sea floor movement (usually an earthquake), not by tides.
mistakes.w: A tsunami is a tidal wave.

summary: You need to know the primary and secondary effects (social, economic and environmental) of tectonic hazards, the immediate and long-term responses, and why impacts and responses differ between rich and poor countries, using case studies of an LIC or NEE and an HIC. It matters because case-study answers earn most of the marks in this topic, and they depend on precise facts and clear comparison.

terms.d: The immediate impact of a tectonic event on people and property, such as collapsing buildings.
An impact that occurs later as a result of the primary effects, such as fires, disease or loss of jobs.
Action taken in the hours, days and first weeks after a hazard to save lives and meet basic needs.
Action taken in the months and years after a hazard to rebuild and reduce future risk.
The size of an earthquake, measured on the Richter (or moment magnitude) scale.
The point underground where an earthquake starts.
The point on the surface directly above the focus.
A smaller earthquake that follows the main earthquake and can cause more damage.
When loose, wet ground behaves like a liquid during shaking, so buildings sink or tilt.
A series of large sea waves caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor, such as an undersea earthquake.
A fast-moving cloud of very hot ash, gas and rock that flows down a volcano's slopes.
A mudflow of volcanic ash mixed with water.
Help, such as money, food, equipment and expertise, given to a country after a disaster.
A non-governmental organisation, such as the Red Cross, that provides aid and is independent of governments.
Rules about how buildings must be constructed, including making them earthquake-resistant.
Payment to cover losses; richer countries rely on it to pay for rebuilding.
Low income country: a country with a low level of development and GDP per person.
High income country: a country with a high level of development and GDP per person.
Teams, often with trained dogs and equipment, that look for people trapped in rubble.
An instrument that detects and records the shaking of an earthquake.

worked.ans: Model answer: In the Christchurch earthquake of 22 February 2011 (magnitude 6.3) the primary effects included 185 deaths and around 2,000 injuries, because the shaking was strong and shallow and buildings such as the CTV building collapsed (1 + 1). The shaking also damaged about 100,000 houses (1). Secondary effects followed: liquefaction of the wet ground covered streets in silt and broke water and sewage pipes, so many homes had no water, and thousands of people left the city because their homes were damaged (1). The clean-up cost was around NZ$40 billion (1).
worked.q: Using a case study of a tectonic hazard in an HIC, explain the primary and secondary effects of the hazard. [4 marks]
steps: Name the case study with date and magnitude: Christchurch earthquake, 22 February 2011, magnitude 6.3.
Primary effects with data: 185 deaths, about 2,000 injured, buildings such as the CTV building collapsed, around 100,000 houses damaged.
Secondary effects: liquefaction damaging roads and pipes, loss of power and water, thousands left the city, costs of about NZ$40 billion.
Link: say how the primary effect leads to a secondary effect (collapsed buildings and damaged pipes led to loss of water and homes).

worked.ans: Model answer: After the 2015 Nepal earthquake (LIC), the immediate response relied heavily on international aid from countries such as India, China and the UK, who sent rescue teams, tents and food (1). However, landslides blocked roads to mountain villages and the airport was overwhelmed, so help reached remote areas slowly and many people dug for survivors by hand (1). In contrast, in Christchurch (HIC) in 2011 well-trained local and national rescue teams were working within hours and a state of emergency was declared (1). The city centre was cordoned off, and water tankers and portable toilets were quickly provided (1). Both received international search and rescue teams (1). The difference is because New Zealand is wealthier, has better equipment, roads and services and had prepared with drills, whereas Nepal has limited resources and difficult mountain terrain (1).
worked.q: Compare the immediate responses to an earthquake in an LIC and an HIC. Use named examples. [6 marks]
steps: Nepal immediate responses: international teams from India, China and the UK; tents, food, water; helicopters; but roads were blocked and supplies were slow.
Christchurch immediate responses: well-practised search and rescue (including international teams), state of emergency, cordon of the centre, water tankers and portable toilets.
Compare: speed, organisation, dependence on foreign aid.
Explain why: development, money, equipment, infrastructure.

worked.ans: About 49 times greater (9,000 / 185 = 48.6, which rounds to 49).
worked.q: The magnitude of the Nepal earthquake was 7.8 and the magnitude of the Christchurch earthquake was 6.3. Deaths were about 9,000 and 185. Calculate how many times greater the number of deaths was in Nepal. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. [2 marks]
steps: Divide the larger number by the smaller: 9,000 divided by 185.
Round to the nearest whole number: 49.
